int cmp_ll(const void*a,const void*b){long long x=*(const long long*)a,y=*(const long long*)b;return x>y?1:x<y?-1:0;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(!n)return 0;long long*a=malloc(sizeof(long long)*n);memcpy(a,v,sizeof(long long)*n);qsort(a,n,sizeof(long long),cmp_ll);long long best=1,run=1;for(int i=1;i<n;i++){run=a[i]==a[i-1]?run+1:1;if(run>best)best=run;}free(a);return best;}

problems.title: Cold Store Aisle Sweep
problems.story: A cold store numbers its aisles outward from the central corridor. The corridor itself is aisle 0, aisles on one side run negative, aisles on the other run positive. During a stock-take a worker logs each aisle as they finish it, in whatever order the aisles happened to be walked. An aisle can be logged more than once if two people covered it, and plenty are never reached at all. What the manager needs before signing off is not how many aisles were done, but the largest stretch that can be certified as a whole.
problems.statement:
You are given the aisle numbers from the log.

An unbroken block is a set of consecutively numbered aisles where every aisle in the set appears in the log at least once. A block with a hole anywhere in it is not unbroken. A single logged aisle is an unbroken block of one.

Return the number of aisles in the largest unbroken block.
problems.inputFormat: Each number is one aisle that was logged. They appear in the order the aisles were walked, which carries no meaning here. The same aisle may appear any number of times, and the log may be empty.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of aisles in the largest unbroken block of consecutively numbered aisles that were all logged. Return 0 for an empty log.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Every aisle number recorded in the stock-take log, in the order it was walked.

constraints: The same aisle number may appear any number of times
The log may be empty, in which case the answer is 0

examples.explanation: The log covers aisles 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 9. Aisles 1 through 4 form an unbroken block of four. Aisle 7 and aisle 9 each stand alone, because 5, 6 and 8 were never logged.
One aisle walked four times is still one aisle. The largest unbroken block has a single member, so the answer is one rather than four.
Aisles -2, -1, 0 and 1 run consecutively across the corridor, which is a block of four. Aisle 3 is cut off because aisle 2 was never logged.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: aisles 1 through 4 are the largest unbroken block.
A block that runs across the corridor from negative aisles into positive ones.
An empty log. Catches a solution that assumes at least one aisle, or that starts its best-so-far at one.
The smallest non-empty log, holding the most negative aisle allowed.
Both constraint extremes present. The two largest aisle numbers are consecutive; the most negative one is isolated.
Seven entries covering four aisles. A solution that measures the run by counting log entries rather than distinct aisles reports 7.
Every entry is the same aisle, so the largest block holds one aisle.
Two blocks interleaved in the log, three aisles and four. Order of logging must not decide the answer.

hints: The order the aisles were walked carries no meaning, so any solution that depends on it is solving a different problem.
Membership is the only question you ever ask of the log: is this aisle number in it or not. A structure that answers that in constant time is the whole tool.
Walking upward from every logged aisle re-walks the same block once per member. Ask which single aisle in a block is worth starting from.
An aisle whose immediate lower neighbour was also logged can never be the bottom of a block, so it is never worth starting a count there.

editorial.overview: The log is a bag of aisle numbers whose order and repetitions carry no information, so the first move is to reduce it to the set of aisles that appear at all. The question then becomes a question about that set: how long is its longest run of consecutive integers.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Put every aisle in a set, then from each aisle walk upward while the next number is present, and keep the longest walk. Without a guard this re-walks a block of length k once from every one of its k members, which is quadratic on a single long block and times out at two hundred thousand aisles.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep the same set, but only start counting at an aisle whose immediate lower neighbour is absent. Such an aisle is the bottom of its block, every block has exactly one bottom, and so every block is walked exactly once. The total work across all walks is therefore the size of the set rather than its square, giving O(n) expected time with a hash set. Sorting the distinct aisles and scanning for consecutive steps is a correct alternative at O(n log n), which also fits comfortably inside the limit.
editorial.correctnessProof: Consider any unbroken block in the set and let b be its smallest member. Then b - 1 is absent, so b is a starting aisle and the walk from b counts the whole block. Conversely a walk started at any aisle a stops as soon as it meets a gap, so it never counts an aisle outside the block containing a, and it never overcounts. Every block therefore contributes its exact length exactly once, and taking the maximum over starting aisles gives the largest block. Duplicates cannot affect the result because the set holds each aisle once, which is why reducing the log to a set is a step of the argument and not an optimisation.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n) expected, where n is the number of logged entries. Each distinct aisle is visited at most twice: once as a candidate start, once inside a single walk.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the set of distinct aisles.

problems.title: Twin Gate Target Pairs
problems.story: Twin Gate Target Pairs is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise distinct target pairs result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Twin Gate Target Pairs. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the distinct target pairs, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values[0] is the target. The remaining elements form the collection to pair.
problems.outputFormat: Return the number of distinct unordered value pairs whose sum equals the target.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: A pair uses two different positions; equal-value pairs need two copies.

examples.explanation: Example 1 follows the stated distinct target pairs process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 3.
Example 2 follows the stated distinct target pairs process. Every contributing value is visible in the input, and the computed result is 2.

testCases.explanation: Applying the distinct target pairs rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.
Applying the distinct target pairs rule to this input produces the stated result without using any unstated data.

hints: Sort the collection and place one pointer at each end.
Move both pointers after a match and skip repeated values so a value pair is counted once.

editorial.overview: Sort the payload values, then converge two pointers according to whether their sum is below, above, or equal to the target.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every pair of positions and store matching value pairs in a set to remove duplicates.
editorial.optimalApproach: A sorted two-pointer scan counts each distinct complement pair once while skipping equal neighbors.
editorial.correctnessProof: At each step, a sum below target cannot be repaired by decreasing the right value, so advancing left loses no solution; the symmetric argument holds above target. A match is counted once and duplicate values are skipped, so every distinct pair appears exactly once.

c11.referenceSolution:
int cmp_ll(const void*a,const void*b){long long x=*(const long long*)a,y=*(const long long*)b;return x>y?1:x<y?-1:0;}
long long solve(const long long*v,int n){if(n<3)return 0;long long*a=malloc(sizeof(long long)*(n-1));memcpy(a,v+1,sizeof(long long)*(n-1));qsort(a,n-1,sizeof(long long),cmp_ll);int l=0,r=n-2;long long c=0;while(l<r){long long s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;long long x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}free(a);return c;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){if(v.empty())return 0;auto a=vector<long long>(v.begin()+1,v.end());sort(a.begin(),a.end());int l=0,r=(int)a.size()-1;long long c=0;while(l<r){auto s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;auto x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}return c;}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){if(v.length==0)return 0;long[]a=Arrays.copyOfRange(v,1,v.length);Arrays.sort(a);int l=0,r=a.length-1;long c=0;while(l<r){long s=a[l]+a[r];if(s==v[0]){c++;long x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]==x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]==y)r--;}else if(s<v[0])l++;else r--;}return c;}

python3.referenceSolution:
def solve(v: list[int]) -> int:
    if not v: return 0
    t,a=v[0],sorted(v[1:]);l,r,c=0,len(a)-1,0
    while l<r:
        s=a[l]+a[r]
        if s==t:
            c+=1;x,y=a[l],a[r]
            while l<r and a[l]==x:l+=1
            while l<r and a[r]==y:r-=1
        elif s<t:l+=1
        else:r-=1
    return c

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){if(!v.length)return 0;const t=v[0],a=v.slice(1).sort((x,y)=>x-y);let l=0,r=a.length-1,c=0;while(l<r){const s=a[l]+a[r];if(s===t){c++;const x=a[l],y=a[r];while(l<r&&a[l]===x)l++;while(l<r&&a[r]===y)r--;}else if(s<t)l++;else r--;}return c;}

problems.title: Kiln Soak Window
problems.story: A studio kiln carries a probe that records the chamber temperature once a minute, from the first flame to the last. Some glazes need a soak: a stretch of the firing where the heat is held as steady as the kiln can manage. What matters to the glaze is not how hot the soak runs. It is how little the temperature moves while the soak lasts.
problems.statement:
You are given a soak length in minutes, followed by the temperature log in the order the probe recorded it.

For any stretch of consecutive readings exactly as long as the soak, call its spread the highest reading in that stretch minus the lowest. A perfectly steady stretch has a spread of zero.

Return the smallest spread of any stretch in the log whose length is exactly the soak length.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the soak length in minutes. Every number after it is one temperature reading, in the order the probe recorded them. The log always holds at least as many readings as the soak is long.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest spread found among all stretches of readings exactly as long as the soak.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The soak length in minutes, followed by the temperature log in recording order.

constraints: The log holds n = values.length - 1 readings, and 1 <= soak length <= n
The answer can exceed the range of a 32-bit signed integer: a log holding both extremes has a spread of 2000000000

examples.explanation: The five stretches of three readings have spreads 3, 14, 14, 4 and 2. The steadiest is the last one, 1052 1051 1053, which moves by two degrees.
A one-minute soak is a single reading, and a single reading cannot move. Every stretch has a spread of zero, so the smallest is zero.
The soak is as long as the whole log, so there is exactly one stretch to consider. Its hottest reading is 1205 and its coolest is 1180, a spread of twenty-five degrees.

testCases.explanation: The worked example: the last three readings move by two degrees.
Soak length equals the log length, so one stretch is the whole log.
The smallest legal input: one reading and a one-minute soak. Catches an implementation that assumes at least two readings.
Both constraint extremes in one stretch. The answer exceeds a 32-bit signed integer.

Every early stretch spans two billion while the answer is two. A solution holding the spread in a 32-bit int overflows on the early stretches and reports a negative value smaller than the true answer.
Every reading is identical, so every stretch is perfectly steady. Catches a deque that mishandles ties when popping.
The steadiest pair is the repeated 6, in the middle rather than at either end.

hints: Every stretch you consider has exactly the same length, so as you step forward one reading joins the stretch and one leaves it.
You never need the whole stretch, only its hottest and coolest reading. Ask what it costs to keep just those two up to date.
A reading that is cooler than one arriving after it can never be the hottest reading of any later stretch. That observation lets you discard it permanently.
Keep two queues of positions, one whose readings decrease and one whose readings increase, and drop the front of each when it falls out of the stretch.

editorial.overview: The stretches all have the same length and move one reading at a time, which is the shape of a sliding window. The work is keeping the hottest and coolest reading of the current window available in constant time, because recomputing them from scratch is what makes the naive solution too slow.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Take every starting position, scan its whole stretch, and track the largest and smallest reading you see. That is O(n * w) time and O(1) extra space. It is correct and it is fine for a short log, but with two hundred thousand readings and a soak half that long it performs roughly ten billion comparisons.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep two double-ended queues of positions rather than values. The first holds positions whose readings strictly decrease from front to back, so its front is always the hottest reading of the current window. The second holds positions whose readings increase, so its front is the coolest. When a reading arrives, pop from the back of each queue while the arriving reading beats what is there, then push its position. Afterwards drop the front of either queue if it has fallen out of the window. Once the first full window is complete, its spread is the difference of the two fronts, and the answer is the smallest such difference. Each position is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole pass is O(n) time and O(n) space.
editorial.correctnessProof: Take the maximum queue. If position i is in the window and some later position j in the window holds a reading at least as hot, then i can never be the answer for this window or any later one, because every later window containing i also contains j. Popping i is therefore safe. What remains is exactly the set of positions not dominated by any later position in the window, and the front of that set is the earliest, which is the current maximum. The minimum queue is the same argument with the comparison reversed. Since the fronts are the true maximum and minimum of each window, the spread computed for each window is exact, and taking the smallest over all windows gives the answer.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the number of readings. Each position enters and leaves each queue at most once.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the two queues of positions, which together hold at most n entries.
